prompt:
An experiment is carried out to determine the volume of a solid cylindrical brass weight.
The known true dimensions of the cylinder are:
True diameter d_true = 12.00 mm
True length L_true = 40.0 mm
Two students, Student A and Student B, measure the cylinder:
- Student A uses a metre rule to measure both diameter and length, recording a single reading for each: d = 12 mm, L = 40 mm.
- Student B uses a micrometer screw gauge to measure diameter and vernier calipers to measure length. However, Student B does not realize that the micrometer has an uncorrected zero error of +0.20 mm. Student B records five diameter readings:
12.21 mm, 12.19 mm, 12.20 mm, 12.21 mm, 12.20 mm.
(a) State the resolution of the metre rule used by Student A and the micrometer screw gauge used by Student B. [2]
(b) Compare the precision of the diameter measurements taken by Student A and Student B, explaining your reasoning. [1]
(c) Calculate the mean diameter recorded by Student B. Explain why Student B's diameter measurement has higher precision but lower accuracy than Student A's measurement. [2]
(d) Describe the corrective action Student B must take to make the diameter measurement both precise and accurate. [1]

parts.description: State resolutions of metre rule and micrometer
Calculate Student B mean and contrast precision with accuracy
Describe corrective action for Student B

part_enrichment.guidance: Metre rule has 1 mm resolution; micrometer has 0.01 mm resolution.
Student B has repeated readings with tiny spread (0.02 mm), whereas Student A took only a single reading with a coarse rule.
Calculate B's mean (12.20 mm). Contrast small spread (high precision) with 0.20 mm offset from true 12.00 mm (low accuracy).
Subtract the +0.20 mm zero error from readings.

mark_scheme.criterion: Part (a): Micrometer screw gauge resolution = 0.01 mm.
Part (b): Student B has higher precision because repeated readings have a tiny range of 0.02 mm (12.21 - 12.19 mm), whereas Student A took only one reading with a coarse instrument.

Part (c): Student B has higher precision due to small spread (0.02 mm), but lower accuracy because the uncorrected positive zero error offsets the mean by +0.20 mm from the true 12.00 mm, whereas Student A's reading (12 mm) matches the true value.
Part (d): Subtract the zero error of +0.20 mm from each reading (giving a corrected mean of 12.00 mm).

hints: In part (a), state standard resolutions in mm.
In part (b), compare spread of repeated readings.
In part (c), calculate the mean for B and compare both students' readings to 12.00 mm.
In part (d), how is a positive zero error corrected?
solution: (a) Metre rule: 1 mm; Micrometer: 0.01 mm. (b) Student B is more precise due to a tiny range of 0.02 mm across repeats. (c) Mean for B = 12.20 mm. B has higher precision (tiny spread) but lower accuracy (offset of +0.20 mm from true 12.00 mm), whereas A's reading (12 mm) matches the true value. (d) Subtract the zero error (+0.20 mm) from all readings.
teacher_walkthrough: (a) Metre rule resolution = 1 mm; micrometer resolution = 0.01 mm.
(b) Precision reflects agreement between repeats. Student B took 5 readings with range 12.21 - 12.19 = 0.02 mm (tight agreement). Student A took only a single reading, showing no repeated precision.

(c) Student B's mean = 12.20 mm. Accuracy is closeness to true value (12.00 mm). Student B is shifted by +0.20 mm due to zero error, so B is less accurate. Student A's reading of 12 mm is close to 12.00 mm (accurate to 2 s.f.).
(d) Correcting the +0.20 mm zero error gives: 12.20 - 0.20 = 12.00 mm, making Student B's measurement both precise and accurate.

provenance.independence_statement: Authored structured scenario comparing two student measurement methodologies for precision, accuracy, and zero error correction.
